sections.h2: Seneca County Recorder: location and role
sections.html:
The Seneca County Recorder works out of the county building at 109 S. Washington Street in Tiffin, the same building that houses the Auditor and the Treasurer. The Recorder's line is 419-447-4434. The office files deeds and mortgages in the order they arrive and marks each with the exact time of presentation, a duty found in ORC 317.13.

The county covers 553 square miles, nearly 80 percent of it farmland, and Tiffin sits on both banks of the Sandusky River. Fostoria and Bellevue each lie partly inside the county line, so expect a deed here to describe anything from a Tiffin bungalow to a few acres on a county road. Population has slipped from 61,901 in 1980 to 55,069 in 2020, and many sellers are heirs or owners of houses that need work. Whatever the condition, the sale ends the same way: a deed stamped at the Auditor and then filed with the Recorder.

sections.h2: Which office gets the deed first?
sections.html:
The Auditor does. Every transfer document has to be presented there before it can be recorded, under ORC 319.203. The Auditor sits in Suite 2206 of the same building, answers at 419-447-0692, and keeps weekday hours.

Bring and pay the following at the Auditor's counter:

  • A conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand dollars conveyed.
  • A transfer fee of fifty cents for each parcel named in the deed.
  • A check made out to the Seneca County Auditor for the correct total. Blank checks are refused, and a wrong amount returns the paperwork unrecorded.
  • The state's DTE 100 form, or DTE 100 (EX) if the transfer qualifies for an exemption. Both are on the Auditor's forms page next to an online fee calculator.

The base figure comes from ORC 319.54(G)(3), which sets the state-level charge. Section 322.02 separately lets a board of county commissioners levy a transfer tax up to thirty cents per hundred. Seneca County uses one combined local rate, so ask the Auditor for the total when you budget for closing.

State law requires the grantor's signature to be acknowledged before an official such as a notary, judge, clerk of a court of record, county auditor, county engineer or mayor, as ORC 5301.01 lists them. That one rule covers deeds, mortgages, land contracts and leases.

Seneca County adds its own demands. The legal description must name the township or the city or village, the county and the state, and carry the right parcel numbers. The Tax Map Office reviews every description, and the wording should match the prior deed or the new survey exactly. The tax map line is 419-448-5719.

Splits are the slow part. A survey is generally needed, and the approving body depends on location: the Seneca Regional Planning Commission outside municipalities, the city engineer inside a city, village council inside a village. After January 1, 2027, splits, resurveys and combinations will appear in property tax records only from tax year 2028. Anyone selling a piece of a larger parcel should start the survey early.

sections.h2: What does recording a deed cost?
sections.html:
The Recorder's fee follows ORC 317.32. For a standard instrument the statute pairs a base fee with a housing trust fund fee, and it allows a county to add a preservation surcharge. Totals differ from county to county, so phone the Seneca County Recorder for the current amount. A short payment can bring the deed back.

Charges tied to a Seneca County deed
ChargeAmountPaid to
Conveyance fee$4.00 per thousand dollars conveyedCounty Auditor
Transfer fee$.50 per parcelCounty Auditor
First two pages recorded$17 base and $17 housing trust fundCounty Recorder
Each page after two$4 base and $4 housing trust fundCounty Recorder
Preservation surchargeUp to $5, if the county adopts itCounty Recorder

Ohio law now requires every recorder to offer electronic recording of real property conveyances and to publish electronic indexes and images for instruments recorded from January 1, 1980 forward, free of any access fee (ORC 317.13). Ask the Seneca County Recorder which e-recording vendor the office uses.

The Auditor's site is the easiest place to start a search. It reaches any parcel by name, address or map and shows the appraisal and payment history. It also publishes a real estate sales report, where sellers can read recent Seneca County sale prices. Five public computers are available in the building: two in the Auditor's office, two with the Treasurer and one at the Recorder.

sections.h2: From signing to a recorded deed
sections.html:
The order of steps rarely changes. The seller signs the deed in front of a notary. The deed and the DTE form go to the Auditor with a check for the conveyance and transfer fees, and the Auditor stamps it. Then the stamped deed goes next door to the Recorder with the recording fee. The Recorder times the filing, indexes it and returns the original.

A title company carries a deed through these steps at a closing. A family member handling a transfer alone can do the same in person, and all three offices are in the same Tiffin building. Before you go, confirm the total with the Auditor and the Recorder, and bring the prior deed so the legal description can be checked against it.

The Recorder can turn a deed away in two situations. ORC 317.13 lets the office refuse an instrument the Revised Code does not require or authorize to be recorded, or one the recorder reasonably believes is materially false or fraudulent. The filer can then ask the common pleas court for an order.

The Auditor values the county's roughly 35,539 parcels and the Treasurer bills and collects. A closing agent asks the Treasurer for the payoff on any half still open, and a seller can look up the payment history on the Auditor's site first.

  • Value complaints go to a three-member Board of Revision. File between January 1 and March 31 with original notarized signatures.
  • A further appeal after the Board rules goes to the state Board of Tax Appeals or the local common pleas court within 30 days of the notice.
  • The homestead exemption for older or disabled owners is filed with the Auditor by December 31. For 2026 bills, new applicants needed $40,000 or less in Ohio adjusted gross household income, and disabled-veteran owners face no income test.

Ohio also has a veteran-related exemption created by House Bill 59 and codified at ORC 5709.17. Ask the Auditor whether a property qualifies before a sale closes.

faqs.q: Do I record a Seneca County deed with the Auditor or the Recorder?
faqs.a: Both, in that order. The Auditor collects the conveyance fees and stamps the deed, then the Recorder files it.

faqs.q: What if my Seneca County deed has the wrong fee on the check?
faqs.a: The paperwork is sent back unrecorded. Incorrect fees and blank checks both cause rejection, so call 419-447-0692 for the amount before you write the check.

faqs.q: Can the Recorder turn down a deed?
faqs.a: Yes, in two situations. The recorder may refuse an instrument the Revised Code does not require or authorize to be recorded, or one believed to be materially false or fraudulent. The filer can ask the common pleas court for an order.

faqs.q: Is an attorney needed to transfer a house in Seneca County?
faqs.a: No law makes one mandatory. Still, the Tax Map Office checks every legal description and a mismatch holds up the sale, so many owners ask a title company or attorney to prepare the deed.

faqs.q: Until when can I contest a Seneca County valuation?
faqs.a: Through March 31 of the year after the tax year in question. Use the Board of Revision complaint form with notarized original signatures. The Auditor at 419-447-0692 can say which tax year applies to your parcel.
